sentence: It sits in the same family of Spanish endearment vocabulary as [mamacita](/mamacita-meaning/), whose Wiktionary entry lists affectionate and slang senses.
note: Target documents affectionate and slang mamacita senses via Wiktionary; comparison is restricted to endearment vocabulary.
target_quote: 'Wiktionary\'s entry for the Spanish suffix -cito describes it as an alternative form of -ito, "added to masculine words and names to denote a diminutive form," used especially "with words ending in a consonant or a vowel other than -o," and, unlike -ito, one that "does not delete the final vowel" of the word it attaches to. The feminine counterpart, -cita, works the same way. In mamacita, -cita follows mamá, giving mamá + -cita = mamacita, "little mama." The masculine parallel is exact: Wiktionary\'s entry for papacito glosses it simply as "diminutive of papá; daddy," built from the identical papá + -cito pattern. Spanish builds a comparable family term the opposite direction, by contraction rather than suffixing: [mijo](/mijo-meaning/) squeezes mi hijo, "my son," into one word used to address a child or close friend, an entirely separate history from the identically spelled word for a cereal grain.',

additional_target_body_support_quotes: 'Wiktionary\'s Spanish-language entry for mamacita doesn\'t treat this as one meaning with a loose figurative extension; it lists two separate senses. The first is simply "diminutive of mamá," unmarked for region or register, the ordinary affectionate word a child might use for their mother. The second is labeled "(Latin America, slang) babe, hottie (sexually attractive woman)," geographically restricted in a way the first sense isn\'t.',
